stem: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the web server process on an instance stops after a memory error, the target group marks the instance unhealthy, and the instance still passes its EC2 status checks. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks
the target group marks the instance unhealthy, and the instance still passes its EC2 status checks

options.text: Leave the health check type of the Auto Scaling group as it is, and rely on the group to replace each instance that it finds unhealthy.
options.why: By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, and the instance passes its EC2 status checks, so it stays in service.

options.text: Install an agent on each instance that tests the web server every minute and reports each failed test to the Auto Scaling API as an unhealthy instance.
options.why: It works, because a custom check can [mark that particular instance as](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-custom-health-check-immediate-replace) unhealthy, but the team builds and runs an agent that one setting replaces.

options.text: Configure the Application Load Balancer to replace each target that fails its health checks with a new instance from the launch template of the group.
options.why: A failed check makes the load balancer [stop routing requests to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-elb-requests-before-detection-fail); launching a replacement is work for the group.

options.text: Set the health check type of the Auto Scaling group to include Elastic Load Balancing, so that the group acts on the health that the target group reports.
options.why: Then [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and the group [replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced), with one setting and no code to run.

explanation: The web server stops while the instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks the instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced) and replaces it.
takeaway: A running instance whose web server failed needs the ELB health check type on the group.
twin: If the stem said "the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check" instead: keep the current settings, because EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default).
say: The group ignores the target group's verdict until you turn on ELB health checks, so I'd turn them on.
